case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
case.limits: Section 230 protects the republication of someone else's content. A generated sentence has no other author to point at, and courts have so far been unwilling to assume the answer.
case.holding: Section 230 bars treating an interactive computer service as the publisher of information provided by another, and notice of the content does not remove that protection.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The foundation of every argument that an AI provider is a conduit for material originating elsewhere. Whether a model output counts as information provided by another information content provider is the unresolved question underneath a growing share of AI defamation claims.

reading.body:
Zeran v. AOL is the precedent every AI defamation defense leans on, yet its protection requires content provided by another, and a model's generated sentence has no other author.

The Fourth Circuit held in 1997 that Section 230 bars treating an interactive computer service as the publisher of information provided by another, and that notice of the content does not remove that protection. For AI providers, the unresolved question is whether a model output counts as information provided by another information content provider. Courts have so far been unwilling to assume the answer.

Six live cases are listed under this precedent, including two against OpenAI entities and four against Character Technologies. The data does not indicate outcomes in those cases, nor whether any court has extended Zeran to generated text. It also does not cover AI liability claims outside the Section 230 publisher question.

section.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
